newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl hopes for progress at tax summit with SPD.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl hopes for progress at tax summit with SPD.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday said tax talks next Monday with opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine were meant to fix the German economy and did not herald a shift in the political landscape.

Shaken by January's half-million surge in unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933 -- both sides have said they are ready to end a standoff and search for a quick deal to avert long and bitter wrangling in parliament.
But, Kohl said, that did not mean he was about to abandon his 14-year-old alliance of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and liberal Free Democrats (FDP) for a grand coalition.

"Monday's talks have nothing to do with a grand coalition," he said in a speech. "The more agreement we can reach, the more we will be able to implement. This would bring a beneficial impetus for the labour market."

With elections looming in 1998, it is unclear just how far Lafontaine will be ready to yield to Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to cut 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) in tax to boost jobs and ensure lasting fitness for European monetary union (EMU).

Thursday's parliamentary debate on the economy gave a mixed reading of SPD intentions. Parliament leader Rudolf Scharping called for Kohl to resign at once,mocking his coalition's "meaningless promises and false starts".
Gerhard Schroeder, SPD premier of Lower Saxony state, struck a more conciliatory note, saying the opposition wanted to help Waigel pass reforms "but not at the price he has set".
Although Schroeder regularly outscores Lafontaine in polls as the favoured SPD challenger to become chancellor next year, he will, significantly, not join the first round of talks.
By then Lafontaine -- also Saarland state premier -- will have recovered from a cold that has sidelined him this week and will take a 10-point shopping list of demands into the talks.
Waigel's strategy plans a two-stage reform, with cuts in corporate taxes starting in 1998 and a drop in income tax in 1999. The cuts would be offset by scrapping 70 tax breaks.
Although no breakthroughs are expected at Monday's talks, which start at 1400 GMT, compromises should be easy to reach on a bottom rate for income tax and on cutting corporate taxes.
Waigel's income tax model sees an entry bracket of 15 percent, down from 26 percent, with a sliding scale from 22.5 to 39 percent. The SPD wants a bottom rate below 20 percent.

But the top rate is problematic. The SPD is resisting a cut to 39 percent from 53 percent sought by Waigel, but also knows that if income and corporate taxes are too far out of line, that could violate the constitution.
The SPD also wants tax relief to stay on night, weekend and holiday shifts -- which Waigel wants to abolish -- and rejects a rise in value-added tax to finance direct tax cuts.
The biggest barrier could be timing. Waigel wants most of the tax cuts to happen in 1999 but the SPD and even the FDP are clamouring for bigger tax cuts a year earlier.
Whether struggling state finances can cope with the extra cuts in 1998, on top of an already-planned reduction in the so-called solidarity surcharge on income tax, is doubtful.
Waigel admitted on Thursday he could only meet his 1997 deficit target of 2.9 percent of GDP if savings measures blocked by the SPD in the Bundesrat upper house were passed.

Kohl said on Friday that Germany and other European states would have to make great efforts to qualify for EMU. A senior central banker said Germany might this year miss the three percent deficit goal set by the Maastricht treaty.
But Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told the Frankfurter Rundschau Bonn would still join EMU's 1999 start.
Despite Kohl's rejection, his heir-apparent Wolfgang Schaueble and Schroeder have been making noises which suggest both sides are ready to link in a grand coalition.
But, Wirtschaftswoche magazine wrote, Waigel sees a more sinister twin strategy behind Lafontaine's readiness to talk.

"In public he supports the euro but in the Bundesrat he is doing everything possible to thwart the attainment of the Maastricht criteria. The goal of the Saarland strategist: If EMU fails, then Kohl has to go," the magazine said.
($ = 1.685 German Marks)
